title: Mountain View Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Mountain View-area wells have a 29 ft median depth. Compare reported yields, $7,400-$14,000 finished-well estimates, permits and buyer risks.
h1: What Mountain View Well Records Mean for Your Property
intro_html:
A shallow well record does not necessarily describe a household water supply. Around Mountain View, 55% of permitted wells are classified as monitoring, compared with 25% domestic or household use. That matters when using the area's 29 ft median depth to plan a purchase or drilling budget.

These figures cover Colorado DWR permit records within 5 miles of Mountain View, including areas around Lakeside, Edgewater and Wheat Ridge. Use them to narrow your investigation, then check wells serving the same purpose and tapping comparable ground near your lot.

sections.heading: Why Mountain View's 29 ft Median Needs Context
sections.html:
Of the area's permit records, 6,425 report total depth. The median is 29 ft, and the middle half run 20-50 ft. That puts much of the recorded drilling at shallow depths, but the heavy monitoring-well presence means this is not a household-well depth forecast.

The 90th-percentile depth is 125 ft, while the deepest record reaches 1,740 ft. Permits include Alluvial and Quaternary Alluvium entries, along with many unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer entries. The cost model assumes Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. Before accepting a bid based on the shallow median, have the driller identify the intended water-bearing formation and compare nearby domestic completion reports. Depth follows the target formation and site conditions, not the town name.

sections.heading: Reported Yield Near Edgewater and Wheat Ridge
sections.html:
Only 319 wells report pump yield, so the yield figures describe a much smaller sample than the depth records. Reported yield has a 12.0 gpm median, with the middle half at 8.0-15.0 gpm. Those results can support household planning, but a recorded drilling-time yield is not a guarantee of sustained supply today.

The lower end deserves attention: 3% report under 1 gpm, and 8% fall in the 1-5 gpm band. A buyer looking at a low-producing well should ask for a current pumping and recovery test, plus a review of storage and peak demand. A strong result in nearby Edgewater or Wheat Ridge does not establish what a particular Mountain View lot will produce.

sections.heading: Shallow Water Readings, Not Proof of a Falling Table
sections.html:
Static water level is the depth to resting water, not the bottom of the well. Among 208 reported readings, the median is 13 ft below ground, and the middle half fall between 10-20 ft. Neither measurement tells you how far the water level will drop while the pump runs.

Decade medians are 15 ft in the 1950s, 18 ft in the 1960s, and 13 ft in both the 2010s and 2020s. This series does not show a steadily dropping water table. It also does not track the same wells through time, so it cannot establish stability at your property. Obtain a current resting level and pumping-level measurement before relying on an older record.

sections.heading: A Permit History Dominated by More Than Household Drilling
sections.html:
The Mountain View search area contains 11,736 DWR permit records, with 5,742 recorded as constructed. Permit issuance reached 2,223 in the 1990s and 2,298 in the 2000s, followed by 1,789 in the 2010s. The 2020s contain 874 permits, and the newest permit year is 2025. These counts are not a tally of completed household wells.

The most active recorded names are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 4,099 entries; Layne, Christensen Co. (Tormoehlen, David A.), with 195; and Ground Exploration Llc (Bender, Joseph T.), with 150. Treat the Authorized label as a records category to investigate, not a residential driller recommendation. Given the monitoring-heavy use mix, confirm that a prospective driller handles domestic supply work and the intended formation.

sections.heading: Budgeting a New Mountain View Well Beyond the Hole
sections.html:
The supplied Denver Basin sedimentary-bedrock model uses $50-$70 per foot. At the area's 29 ft median depth, that puts the drilled hole around $1,400-$2,000. The modeled finished well, including pump, tank, trenching and electrical, is about $7,400-$14,000.

Those figures are a starting allowance, not a parcel quote. The 20-50 ft middle depth range suggests relatively limited footage for many recorded wells, but monitoring wells can make that comparison misleading for a new household supply. Ask for a written scope identifying casing, grout, development, testing and equipment, along with exclusions. Rig access, the route to the house and a deeper target formation can change the job substantially even when the mapped neighboring wells look shallow.

sections.heading: Environmental Flags and Supply Risks Around Mountain View
sections.html:
Within about 10 miles, the map identifies 660 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 89 historic mine features and 187 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These are screening flags, not proof that a particular well is contaminated. A sampling location may not represent a confirmed detection, and proximity alone does not establish a groundwater pathway.

For a purchase, obtain current laboratory testing and use nearby site information to discuss targeted testing with the laboratory or an environmental professional. Review casing, grout and the wellhead's condition. Low yield or a dry hole remains a site-specific risk; the area's median cannot rule either out. Where septic is proposed, verify that the lot can accommodate the well, wastewater system, building footprint and required separation before finalizing the layout.

sections.heading: Before Closing on a Mountain View Lot
sections.html:
Start with the actual DWR permit and completion report, not a listing that simply says the property has a well. Confirm the permitted uses, construction status and connection to the property being sold. An exempt household-use permit does not automatically authorize outdoor irrigation or every planned use.

Then compare nearby domestic wells rather than pooling all monitoring records into your decision. Lakeside, Edgewater and Wheat Ridge provide local context, but formation and well purpose matter more than a nearby town label. For an existing supply, obtain pumping results, laboratory results and equipment information. For a build, resolve permit eligibility, access, utilities and septic feasibility before committing to the house location. Over-appropriated basin rules and any augmentation requirements need parcel-specific review.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Mountain View, Colorado?
faq.a: Within 5 miles of Mountain View, reported well depth has a 29 ft median, with the middle half at 20-50 ft. The 90th percentile is 125 ft. However, 55% of permits are for monitoring wells, so these figures are not a reliable household drilling target without comparing nearby domestic wells and their formations.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Mountain View?
faq.a: The supplied cost model uses $50-$70 per foot for Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the recorded 29 ft median, the hole is about $1,400-$2,000, while a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $7,400-$14,000. A domestic well targeting deeper water needs a site-specific quote rather than this shallow-depth allowance.

faq.q: How much water do Mountain View wells produce?
faq.a: The 319 records reporting pump yield have a 12.0 gpm median and an 8.0-15.0 gpm middle range. Reported yields under 1 gpm account for 3%. These are historical results from a limited sample, not a supply guarantee. Before buying, request a current pumping and recovery test and check whether storage matches household demand.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Mountain View?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from a permit or depth record. The surrounding map includes 660 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 187 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles, but those counts do not prove contamination in your well. Obtain current laboratory testing and review nearby environmental records to decide which additional contaminants to test.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Mountain View, Colorado?
faq.a: The available decade medians do not show a steady decline: resting water was 15 ft below ground in the 1950s, 18 ft in the 1960s, and 13 ft in both the 2010s and 2020s. These are different groups of measurements, not continuous monitoring of the same wells. Check current resting and pumping levels on the property.
